structures.title: State a basic affirmative fact
structures.explanation: English is a fixed word-order language: the subject comes first, then the verb, then the object. This order rarely changes, so keeping it is the key to being understood. Add -s to the verb only for he/she/it.
structures.ex1_ref: A simple statement of a routine.
structures.ex2_target: She reads the newspaper in the morning.

structures.title: Ask a yes/no or wh- question
structures.explanation: To ask a question in the present or past simple, put the auxiliary do/does/did before the subject and keep the main verb in its base form. Use 'does' for he/she/it and 'did' for the past. The main verb never takes an ending here.
structures.ex1_ref: A yes/no question in the present.
structures.ex2_ref: A wh- question; 'live' stays in base form after 'does'.

structures.title: Make a negative statement
structures.explanation: Negate the present or past simple with do/does/did + not before the base verb. Use 'doesn't' for he/she/it and 'didn't' for the past. The main verb loses its ending because the auxiliary already shows tense and person.

structures.title: Link a past action to now
structures.explanation: The present perfect connects a past event to the present moment. Use have (or has for he/she/it) plus the past participle. It fits experiences, recent actions, and unfinished time periods.
structures.ex1_target: I have visited Paris three times.
structures.ex1_ref: Life experience with no specific date.
structures.ex2_ref: A very recent action, still relevant now.

structures.title: Focus on the action, not the doer
structures.explanation: The passive voice puts the receiver of the action in the subject position. Form it with be (in any tense) plus the past participle, adding 'by + agent' only when it matters. Use it when the doer is unknown, obvious, or unimportant.
structures.ex1_ref: The book matters more than the author here.
structures.ex2_target: English is spoken all over the world.
structures.ex2_ref: The doer is everyone, so it is left out.

structures.title: Report what someone said
structures.explanation: To report speech, use a verb like said, told, or asked, then a clause with the tense shifted one step back. 'That' is optional after said/told. Reported questions use statement word order, with 'if/whether' for yes/no questions.
structures.ex1_ref: Original 'I am tired' shifts to 'she was tired'.
structures.ex2_target: He asked if I could help.
structures.ex2_ref: 'Can you help?' becomes an 'if' clause with no inversion.

structures.pattern: Clause + to / in order to / so that + purpose
structures.title: Explain the reason for an action
structures.explanation: To express purpose, use 'to' or 'in order to' + base verb, or 'so that' + a clause with a modal. This answers the question 'why?'. 'To + verb' is the shortest and most common option.
structures.ex1_target: I study English to get a better job.
structures.ex1_ref: 'to get' explains the purpose of studying.
structures.ex2_target: She left early so that she could catch the train.

structures.title: Concede an unexpected contrast
structures.explanation: These link two facts where the second is surprising given the first. 'Although' and 'even though' are followed by a full clause; 'despite' and 'in spite of' are followed by a noun or -ing form. They can begin or join the sentence.
structures.ex1_target: Although it was raining, we went out.
structures.ex1_ref: 'Although' + clause; the outing is unexpected in the rain.
structures.ex2_target: Despite the rain, we went out.

structures.title: Compare two things
structures.explanation: Compare two things with a comparative adjective plus 'than'. Add -er to short adjectives and use 'more' before longer ones. Never use both -er and 'more' together.
structures.ex1_target: She is taller than her brother.
structures.ex2_target: This phone is more expensive than that one.

structures.title: Add information about a noun
structures.explanation: A relative clause identifies or describes a noun. Use 'who' for people, 'which' for things, and 'that' for either in a defining clause. The relative pronoun replaces the subject or object, so don't repeat it.
structures.ex1_target: The woman who called you is my sister.
structures.ex1_ref: 'who called you' tells us which woman.
structures.ex2_target: The car that he bought is red.
structures.ex2_ref: 'that he bought' identifies the car; 'that' can be dropped as the object.

structures.pattern: If + past simple, would + base verb
structures.title: Imagine an unreal situation
structures.explanation: The second conditional describes an unlikely or imaginary present or future. Use 'if + past simple' in the condition and 'would + base verb' in the result. The past form signals 'unreal', not past time.
structures.ex1_target: If I had more time, I would travel more.
structures.ex1_ref: I don't have the time, so this is imaginary.
structures.ex2_target: If she were here, she would know what to do.
structures.ex2_ref: Use 'were' for all subjects in this pattern.

structures.title: Say that something exists
structures.explanation: Use 'there is' with a singular or uncountable noun and 'there are' with a plural noun to state that something exists. 'There' is a dummy subject with no real meaning here. The verb agrees with the noun that follows.
structures.ex1_target: There is a problem with the plan.
structures.ex2_target: There are two options to choose from.

structures.title: Pick the top of a group
structures.explanation: The superlative shows the extreme of three or more things. Add -est to short adjectives and use 'most' before longer ones, always with 'the'. Use 'in' for places and 'of' for groups.
structures.ex1_target: She is the tallest in the class.
structures.ex2_target: This is the most expensive option.

structures.title: Describe an action happening now
structures.explanation: The present continuous shows an action in progress at the moment of speaking or a temporary situation. Form it with am/is/are + the -ing form of the verb. It contrasts with the present simple, which is for habits.
structures.ex1_ref: An action in progress at this moment.
structures.ex2_target: They are studying for their exams this week.
structures.ex2_ref: A temporary situation, not a permanent habit.

structures.pattern: If + present simple, will + base verb
structures.title: Predict a real future result
structures.explanation: The first conditional describes a real, likely future situation and its result. Use 'if + present simple' for the condition and 'will + base verb' for the result. Note that the 'if' clause uses the present even though it refers to the future.
structures.ex1_target: If it rains, we will stay home.
structures.ex1_ref: A real possibility for the near future.
structures.ex2_target: If you study hard, you will pass the exam.
structures.ex2_ref: 'if you study' (present) leads to 'you will pass'.

structures.title: Ask a polite indirect question
structures.explanation: An indirect question is wrapped inside a polite opener like 'Can you tell me...' or 'Do you know...'. The embedded part keeps statement word order — no inversion and no do/does/did. This sounds more polite than a direct question.
structures.ex1_target: Can you tell me where the station is?
structures.ex1_ref: 'where the station is', not 'where is the station'.
structures.ex2_target: Do you know what time it opens?
structures.ex2_ref: 'what time it opens' keeps subject-verb order.
